newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes weaker in U.S. on French EMU opposition.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes weaker in U.S. on French EMU opposition.

text.p: The dollar ended U.S. trade lower Thursday amid fears Europe's proposed single currency was unravelling and suspicion that global economic leaders might move to weaken the greenback after a Sunday meeting.
A poll showing rising French displeasure with proposed European Monetary Union drove investors to the mark, reversing modest overnight dollar/mark gains, dealers said.
"There is fear that EMU won't come about and that will lead to unwinding of dollar positions against the mark," said Diego Giurleo, vice president of treasury at Royal Bank of Canada in New York.
A Louis Harris poll showed most French voters believe European Monetary Union will threaten jobs and economic growth and 69 percent want a fresh vote on EMU, which France narrowly approved in 1992.
Rejection of EMU, which would combine the French franc with the stronger German mark and other units, could spark heavy selling of francs for marks and dollars, traders said.

"I still think there's some pretty good risk in France. To me, the uncertainty hasn't yet been priced in in this market," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
The dollar fell to 1.7145/55 marks from 1.7185/95 at the open and to 126.03/13 yen from 126.08/18.

The mark crosses gained on news of the French polls, since many investors believe EMU would weaken the German economy to the benefit of its European counterparts. Mark/Paris ended near 3.3750 in the U.S., up from 3.37 in early U.S. trade.
That kept a lid on the dollar, which had risen against the mark early in European trading.
"If France decides EMU is a non-starter, we're going to throw the whole thing out and that would temper upward dollar momentum," said Giurleo.
The dollar rose toward 1.72 marks in morning trade after Germany reported its inflation fell in April.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said he saw no current inflation danger, but noted that any cuts in interest rates would be risky at this time.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer later echoed Krupp's comments, adding that he was generally satisfied with current foreign exchange rates.
Dollar/yen got a minor boost in late New York trading on a Japanese news report that Japan's Ministry of Finance was set to order the closure of Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co.
That would be the first time since World War II that a Japanese life insurer had failed and the report deepened fears about Japan's prolonged economic malaise.
"It's not a really big company, but the dollar was well-bid against the yen after the news," said Masashi Ehara, assistant vice president in foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.

Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer triggered sales of U.S. Treasuries by saying the Fed needs to be "pre-emptive" with monetary policy. But the dollar paid little heed to the apparent hint at higher interest rates, traders said.

Despite the heavy news flow, trade was light. Investors were unwilling to bet aggressively on the dollar ahead of a meeting on Friday between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Investors also awaited a Sunday meeting of economic officials of the Group of Seven nations, which some feared might yield a statement calling for the dollar/yen weakness.

The dollar fell to 1.4603/13 Swiss francs from 1.4660/70 but rose to Canadian $1.3923/28 from C$1.3913/18. Sterling rose to $1.6260/70 from $1.6225/30. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7762/67 from $0.7755/60. --C. Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664
